results.explanation: The source-visible entry is POST /signin. Password authentication is controlled by ENABLE_PASSWORD_AUTH; false produces HTTP 403 ACTION_PROHIBITED. When WEBUI_AUTH_TRUSTED_EMAIL_HEADER is configured, the handler requires that header (otherwise HTTP 400 INVALID_TRUSTED_HEADER), lowercases its value, and passes it to email-based user authentication. If authentication returns a user, the handler creates a session; if it does not, the visible result is HTTP 400 INVALID_CRED. The environment source shows that the trusted header name is deployment-configured through WEBUI_AUTH_TRUSTED_EMAIL_HEADER. Thus the application-source capability to turn a received trusted-email header into the principal and session is shown, but the actual deployment decision is unknown: the supplied source contains no deployment facts establishing whether password sign-in is enabled, whether the header name is configured, whether an external client can reach the application through the relevant ingress, or whether a trusted reverse proxy is the sole ingress that strips client identity headers and injects the authenticated identity. The minimum deployment observations are those configuration values plus ingress topology/header-handling and whether the client-supplied header reaches the application. No repository-wide completeness or deployment reachability is inferred.

facts.statement: The supplied handler defines POST /signin and receives the request, response, sign-in form, and database session.
When password authentication is disabled, the handler raises HTTP 403 with ACTION_PROHIBITED before the trusted-header logic.
The trusted-email header path is enabled only when WEBUI_AUTH_TRUSTED_EMAIL_HEADER is truthy; the header name is supplied by an environment variable and defaults to unset.
When configured, the handler requires the named request header and otherwise raises HTTP 400 with INVALID_TRUSTED_HEADER.
The supplied trusted-email header value is lowercased and assigned as the email used for identity lookup/authentication.
The email value is passed to email-based authentication; if no existing user is found, the shown code invokes signup before authentication.
When authentication returns a user, the handler creates a session response and sets a cookie.
When no user is returned, the visible terminal behavior is HTTP 400 with INVALID_CRED.
The supplied crop omits the other sign-in-mode code, so it does not show an alternative status for the unconfigured-header branch.

Whether an external client can supply the identity header to the application is a deployment-boundary fact; the supplied source does not establish sole-ingress, header-stripping, header-injection, or client-to-application reachability.

branchResults.explanation: With the trusted-header path entered but email authentication producing no user, the visible terminal behavior is HTTP 400 with INVALID_CRED; the session-creation effect is not reached.

If the configured trusted-email header reaches the application without trusted-ingress enforcement and email authentication returns a user, the application lowercases the header value, uses it for email authentication, and creates a session for that user. The source therefore exposes the application capability; deployment reachability is supplied only by the counterfactual assumption.

The trusted-email branch is guarded by the configured header-name value. When it is unconfigured, that branch is not entered, so the supplied source does not establish trusted-header impersonation. The omitted sign-in-mode code prevents asserting a more specific alternative status.
The sign-in handler immediately raises HTTP 403 with ACTION_PROHIBITED when password authentication is disabled, before the trusted-header path can authenticate a user.

Under the accepted policy, trusted-header authentication is safe when a trusted reverse proxy is the sole reachable ingress, removes client-supplied identity headers, and injects the authenticated identity. With that trusted-ingress condition true, an unauthenticated external client cannot choose the principal through a client-supplied header, although the application can still consume the proxy-injected header.
